meta.title: Working in Kanso — Kanso
meta.description: List, board and timeline are one query drawn three ways. The filter language, saved views, the keyboard, scheduling, cycles, workload, triage and the public roadmap.
head.title: One query, three drawings, and four screens that ask something else.
head.lead: The list, the board and the timeline are not three features kept in step. They are one scoped query rendered three ways, which is why a filter typed in one of them is still true in the next.
drawings.title: Three drawings of one query
drawings.body: Pick a scope — a team, a project, a cycle, a person — narrow it with a filter, and then choose how to look at it. One chord cycles list, board and timeline, and the selection survives the change.
drawings.list.label: List
drawings.list: Rows, grouped and folded. The densest of the three and the one the keyboard is designed for.
drawings.board.label: Board
drawings.board: One column per status of the team. Dragging a card changes the status, and nothing else.
drawings.timeline.label: Timeline
drawings.timeline: Bars over weeks, the dependencies drawn between them, and a warning where two overlap.
drawings.wide: Above one team, a board cannot have one column per status — two teams may share no word at all. So a wider board stacks by meaning, the five categories both vocabularies have, and a drop is rebased onto each card's own team's word. Moving between two words that mean the same thing needs a board scoped to one team.
filter.title: The filter language
filter.body: / opens the filter box. It is one line of text, it completes as you type, and what it writes is what it parses — so a filter can be read, copied and pasted between people.
filter.fields: The fields are status:, meaning:, priority:, assignee: (including assignee:me), project:, cycle: and label:. A leading - negates: -priority:low. A chip prints a name, the text prints a token, and both come off the same catalogue so they cannot disagree.
filter.meaning: status: and meaning: are not two spellings of one thing. status: asks for a word one team uses. meaning:started asks the question status: cannot: everything under way, in every team, whatever each one calls it.
views.title: Saved views
views.body: A scope, a filter, a grouping and a drawing, kept under a name. Saved views are how a recurring question stops being retyped — a team's incoming bugs, one person's week, everything blocked — and they are per team rather than global, so they speak that team's vocabulary.
views.where: The sidebar's Saved views row lists them; opening one restores everything it stored, including which of the three drawings it was saved in.
keys.title: The keyboard
keys.body: The same keys in all three drawings. They are not a shortcut layer over a mouse interface — the list is built to be driven this way, and the mouse is what works too.
keys.digits: Your team's first six statuses, in its own order
keys.status: Pick a status by name, including a seventh
keys.help: Every shortcut, as this account has them bound
keys.remap: Every one of them is remappable, per account, and ? prints the bindings in force rather than a picture of the defaults. What is stored is the overrides alone — an account that never changed anything stores nothing, and inherits an improved default instead of a frozen copy of an old one.
schedule.title: Dates, dependencies and the cascade
schedule.body: A blocks edge is one finish-to-start arrow. Moving a date does not push the direct successors and stop: it settles the whole connected component around the change, because a diamond has a ticket whose two predecessors are both in the blast radius and settling it against one would leave the other violated. Three rules decide what actually moves.
schedule.slack: Slack is respected. A successor that still starts after its predecessor ends does not move, and the descent stops there. Without this, every micro-adjustment would creep the whole graph forward and no ticket would ever have slack.
schedule.forward: Nothing is ever pulled backwards. Freeing slack does not drag work into the past — nobody expects it and nobody could undo it.
schedule.done: A done ticket never moves. Its edge is reported violated instead: a plan that claims to hold when it does not is the worst outcome available.
schedule.critical: The critical path is computed per connected component, never per project and never over what is currently on screen — a chain can span three projects, and anchoring on the visible scope would repaint identical data every time the filter changes.
schedule.notion: A date edited in Notion goes through the same engine: the poller writes the scalar and then cascades, so a date typed into the mirror cannot break the plan in silence.
cycles.title: Cycles
cycles.body: A cycle is a dated window of work for one team. The screen answers three questions — how far it has got, what is left, and what will not fit — and every number on it arrives already derived from one endpoint, so the percentage in the header and the list of slipping tickets underneath cannot disagree.
cycles.rollover: Closing a cycle carries its unfinished work into the next one and says so in the activity feed. Velocity is measured from closed cycles; a person may declare one to start with, and it is used only until two closed cycles can answer better — two numbers answering the same question and disagreeing is a tool that lies, so exactly one of them is ever the one being planned with.
workload.title: Workload
workload.body: Open tickets per person, each bar cut by status and drawn long in proportion to the heaviest person's count. It answers who is carrying more than whom, which is a question a count can settle — rather than pretending to measure hours.
workload.points: Points sit beside the count rather than replacing it, and every row showing a total in points also shows how many of its tickets are not in that total. A sum that quietly leaves out the unestimated half of a plate is worse than a count that never claimed to weigh anything.
triage.title: Triage
triage.body: The queue of everything nobody has ruled on yet. It is a gate, not a view: a ticket leaves it because somebody decided, and the decision is one of four words. Similar tickets are offered beside each one, which is what makes the duplicate ruling cheap.
triage.duplicate: It is that other ticket, and the link says which.
triage.record: Each ruling is recorded as a decision rather than applied as a silent edit — which is what makes it safe to hand the queue to an agent. The same four words are the whole vocabulary of the kanso_triage tool.
inbox.title: Inbox and realtime
inbox.body: Mentions, assignments and replies land in the inbox, reachable from the bell in the top bar with its unread count. It is a list of things that happened to you, not a feed of everything.
inbox.realtime: Boards and lists update themselves. Every write publishes on a Postgres channel, every API instance receives it and pushes to its own clients over one WebSocket, and the session cookie that authenticated the page authenticates the socket — so there is no second login and no polling loop.
progress.title: Progress, and the shop window
progress.body: Per person and per team, over closed cycles: what was delivered, at what rate, and what the charts can and cannot speak for. The same rule as everywhere else — a number that could not be computed is absent rather than zero.
progress.roadmap: /roadmap is the one page a stranger may read. It draws the tickets somebody explicitly marked public — the default is private, so publishing is an act, never a state a row drifted into — in the application's own statuses, with nothing reworded for the shop window. Votes help with the ordering; they do not commit to a date.
